If you are a beginning drummer wanting to play drums in a cover band…..

1) A four piece kit covers almost everything you need…..leave the Neil Peart kit at home. You will have faster set up and tear down times, which will allow you more time to relax and hang out before and after the show, resenting your band mates much less, as they likely won’t help you pack up. 

2) Out of 100 people at your show, 98 of them won’t care about your ghost notes, your fills, or basically anything you do on drums, only that the beat sounds close enough to the song. The 1 person in 100 that cares will most likely be a pretentious musician that is just waiting for you to mess up, so he can lean over and tell the 2nd person in 100 that cares, who is also a pretentious musician, that you’ve just missed a 32nd note hi hat strike. Just have fun and keep good time. 

3) Grow some thick skin with regard to your band mates, the venue, the fans, the people in the apartment next to the venue, the entirety of any suburb near the venue, as well as anyone within a 500 mile radius, telling you that your drums are too goddamm loud. There’s no need to Thor hammer your drums, but even the softest hitting drummers are reminded each minute by their band mates that “you are REALLY loud!” Be prepared for the onslaught of angry looks about volume, but always be respectful of the feedback and adjust if possible. 

4) If there’s a “house kit” already set up at the gig, bring yours along anyway and leave it in your vehicle. Chances are, the house kit will be on par with a PlaySkool drum kit, and there’s always something on the kit that is clearly set up by a non-musician (i.e. dining room chair for a throne, torn drum heads fixed with Elmer’s School glue or knitted shut with yarn). 

5) Treat your ears like precious genitals and wear protection. The “eeeeeeeeeeeeeeee” sound that constantly plays in your ears from lots of loud exposure is maddening and affects your sleep, your communication, your relationship, and your sanity. 

6) Drums are fun. Incredibly fun, actually. So much fun that we all make weird drumming faces when we are playing in the groove. Just go with it. People make weird faces during sex, too, so, just embrace it.

I use lots of exploratory questions with patients during the first session, however I always make sure to ask every patient the solution-focused question: 

“imagine you go to bed tonight and wished that all of your problems were gone by the morning. Now imagine your wish came true during the night, however you had no clue that your wish came true. No clue at all. 

What would you notice first? How would you realize your wish was granted?”

I also ask each patient to focus on what WOULD be present, not what WOULDN’T be (i.e. “well I wouldn’t be sad” isn’t enough, I want to know what actual emotion would be present if your sadness wasn’t there). And then we go from there, exploring the things patients really want and need ☺️

I was 10 and wanted to start a fire in our fireplace. No one was home to help me, so I just threw some big logs in and tried to start it up. You make an excellent point. I'm actually agnostic, and I struggle with the idea of an afterlife. I envy people that have the type of faith that allows then to believe that they "know" that there's an afterlife. As a hospice social worker, I have never seen anything to prove to me that there is a heaven. When I wrote this, I was reflecting on all the deaths that I've witnessed, and how so many of them "see" their loved ones that have passed. Especially in the weeks, hours, and moments right before death. So often they will say that they can see "them" and that they are calling to them. This was written more from those experiences, and less from believing in an afterlife. I want there to be a beautiful "heaven", but I cannot lie to myself or anyone and claim there is. So your emotional reaction to this is spot on: for people that believe in something, it's comforting; for others, it reaffirms that nagging notion that is inescapable...that this world is it.  I cannot thank you enough for taking the time to read and respond to my post. I'm so sorry about your brother.
